blocks.text: 1. Feature Maps

blocks.alt: A filter applied to the image produces a feature map

blocks.text: Receptive Field, the previous topic, covered how much of the original input influences one output value. Feature Maps take a closer look at the outputs a convolutional layer actually produces, explored in full depth throughout this topic.
A feature map is the genuinely direct result of sliding one specific filter across an input, already introduced briefly throughout earlier topics in this module, and covered here in complete depth.
2. The Definition, In Full
This connects back to the weighted sum computation, already covered in the Convolution Operation. Every single output value produced by sliding one filter across the input forms a feature map.

This is a genuinely new grid of numbers, just like the original image, already covered in Image Representation, but now representing where and how strongly that specific filter's pattern was detected.

blocks.text: 3. One Filter, One Feature Map

blocks.alt: One filter produces one feature map

blocks.text: This connects back to multiple filters per layer, already covered in Filters and Kernels. Each individual filter genuinely produces its own separate feature map, entirely independent from every other filter's own output.
A layer with 32 filters genuinely produces 32 separate feature maps, each one representing a genuinely different pattern that layer has learned to detect.
4. What A Feature Map Genuinely Encodes

blocks.alt: A feature map encodes where a pattern appears

blocks.text: A genuinely important interpretive idea follows. A genuinely high value at a specific position in a feature map means that filter's specific pattern was genuinely strongly detected right there.
A genuinely low or negative value means that pattern was genuinely absent, or even contradicted, at that position, giving every single feature map a genuinely meaningful, interpretable structure.
5. Stacking Feature Maps Together

blocks.alt: Many feature maps get stacked into a volume

blocks.text: This connects back to the image shape convention, already covered in Image Representation. All of a layer's feature maps genuinely stack together, forming the depth dimension of the output, just like color channels did for the original image.
This stacked output then genuinely becomes the input to the very next layer, exactly the mechanism already covered as filter depth matching input channels in Filters and Kernels.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This stacking, already covered in this topic, is exactly why filter depth must match the input's own number of channels, already covered in Filters and Kernels: each layer's stacked feature maps become the next layer's own input channels.

blocks.text: 6. Early Versus Later Feature Maps

blocks.alt: Early feature maps hold simple patterns while later ones hold complex patterns

blocks.text: This connects back to early versus later layer filters, already covered in Filters and Kernels. Early layer feature maps genuinely highlight simple patterns, like edges, directly reflecting those simpler, early filters.
Later layer feature maps genuinely highlight increasingly complex, abstract patterns, directly reflecting the increasingly complex filters already covered as characteristic of deeper network layers.
7. Visualizing Feature Maps

blocks.alt: A feature map gets visualized as an image

blocks.text: A genuinely useful, real practical technique connects back to interpreting a network's own learned behavior. Displaying a feature map as a genuinely grayscale image directly reveals what that specific filter responds to.

This turns an otherwise abstract grid of numbers, already covered throughout this topic, into a genuinely visual, interpretable picture, a widely used practical technique for understanding what a trained network has actually learned.
8. Recapping Feature Map Dimensions

blocks.alt: A feature map has height, width, and depth

blocks.text: This connects back to Padding and Stride, both already covered in their own topics. A feature map's own height and width, already covered, depend directly on padding and stride, exactly as covered in those two topics.
Its genuinely total count within a layer depends directly on the number of filters, already covered in this topic, giving a genuinely complete picture of how a layer's output shape gets determined.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Why Understanding Feature Maps Genuinely Matters

Debugging or interpreting what a Convolutional Neural Network has genuinely learned is a direct case where visualizing feature maps, already covered in this topic, directly reveals this to a genuinely practical degree.

Reasoning about a network's own internal representations at any given layer is another genuine case where Feature Maps, already covered, are genuinely the concrete, literal form those representations take.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A feature map is the direct output produced by sliding one specific filter across an input.
Each filter produces its own separate feature map; a layer with N filters produces N feature maps.
A high value in a feature map means that filter's pattern was strongly detected at that position.
All of a layer's feature maps stack together, forming the depth dimension passed to the next layer.
Early layer feature maps highlight simple patterns; later layer feature maps highlight complex, abstract ones.
Visualizing a feature map as a grayscale image reveals what its filter responds to.
A feature map's height and width depend on padding and stride; its count depends on the number of filters.
